pages.headline: Grow the firm without betting it on the market for proven consultants.
pages.outcome: Your growth plan currently has one engine: hire consultants whose networks arrive with them, and the market rarely sells one at a price the model affords. Governed AI adds a second engine. Market mapping, drafting, assembly, and reporting move onto rails, consultant attention returns to candidates, clients, and judgment, and each desk runs more searches well without the firm's name or its network paying for it.
triggers: The growth plan assumes hiring proven consultants with portable networks, and every year the market proves it will not supply them at that price.
Consultants are at their search ceiling while mandate demand keeps arriving, and the choice reads as decline work or let coverage and cadence slip.
The firm's market knowledge lives in a few heads and a database nobody fully trusts, and succession is a hope rather than a plan.
Clients have started asking how the firm uses AI and how candidate data is protected, and the answer depends on who they ask.

evidence.text: Enterprise surveys in 2025 find regular AI use near nine in ten organizations, while only a minority report enterprise-level earnings impact and most experiments never fully scale.
evidence.source: McKinsey State of AI 2025; Deloitte generative-AI survey 2025
evidence.caveat: Self-reported, large-enterprise-skewed consultancy surveys, none of them about search firms. The pattern argues for operating discipline and measurement, not for urgency theater; no comparable primary evidence exists for executive search economics.

evidence.text: In a preregistered experiment published in Science in 2023, access to a general AI assistant cut time on occupation-specific professional writing tasks by about 40 percent and raised judged quality by about 18 percent, across roughly 453 college-educated professionals.
evidence.caveat: Controlled, task-level writing results, evaluator-scored; not search deliverables, client mandates, or firm-level capacity. It locates the drafting layer as the opportunity; only your own baseline shows what it returns.

evidence.text: The field experiment that reported gains from AI on tasks inside its capability frontier also reported professional quality falling when consultants relied on it for tasks outside that frontier.
evidence.caveat: Task-level evidence from one elite consulting firm, not a search firm, and the frontier moves with the model and the domain. In search the clearest outside-frontier move is letting a model make reject decisions; the control is a human verdict on every cut, not prohibition.

pages.headline: One governed platform, instead of a sprawl holding fragments of the network.
pages.outcome: The desks are already using AI, approved or not, and some of it is touching candidate data. The question on your desk is whether that becomes a platform the firm can operate and defend, or a sprawl it gets blamed for. Governed AI operations gives you the architecture: mandate-scoped access, approved sources, provenance and retention by default, and a sanctioned path fast enough that nobody wants the shadow one.
triggers: Shadow AI is already in the building: individual subscriptions and browser tools, and nobody can say what candidate data has touched them.
Desks and sector teams are picking point tools independently, each holding fragments of the network with no shared control model.
Client security and data questionnaires have started asking AI questions the current estate cannot answer cleanly.
Leadership wants AI rolled out, and technology is expected to make it safe after the fact.

evidence.text: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (January 2023) and its Generative AI Profile (July 2024) give a voluntary, vendor-neutral scaffold for governing AI design, deployment, use, and evaluation.
evidence.caveat: Voluntary frameworks, not mandates and not a safe harbor. They still have to be adapted to candidate-data obligations, cross-border rules, and each client's expectations of discretion.

pages.headline: Candidate data handling your firm could explain to its most demanding client.
pages.outcome: The risk is not that the firm uses AI. It is that the firm cannot say where candidate data goes, how long it is kept, or whether a model ever influenced who left a list. Governed AI operations replaces improvisation with a defensible posture: mandate boundaries in both directions, human verdicts by explicit rule, retention decided rather than defaulted, and a disclosure answer ready before anyone asks.
triggers: A near-miss surfaced: candidate notes or a client spec in an unapproved tool, caught by luck rather than by design.
A client asked how candidate data is protected, and the answer had to be assembled overnight.
Retention has never been decided, so candidate files accumulate by default, including notes on people who never asked to be in them.
Nobody can say with confidence whether software ever influenced a reject decision, and the regulatory exposure runs in both directions.

evidence.text: The U.S. EEOC and Department of Justice have warned that employers' use of AI and automated software tools in hiring, monitoring, pay, or promotion decisions can violate the Americans with Disabilities Act.
evidence.source: U.S. EEOC and Department of Justice
evidence.caveat: A warning and technical assistance, not a finding that any specific tool is unlawful, and not legal advice. A search firm sits on both sides of it, screening in its own process and advising clients who screen in theirs, which is why reject decisions stay human.

pages.headline: An AI investment case built on your own searches, because there is no benchmark to borrow.
pages.outcome: You have seen the vendor math: day-one payback, hours saved that nobody redeployed, benefits counted three times. In this industry there is not even a credible benchmark to borrow, which makes discipline the whole case. The governed version is different by construction: baselines before pilots, program cost counted once, adoption lag priced in, ranges instead of points, and freed consultant hours named to a destination so they land in fees instead of evaporating.
triggers: AI spend is accumulating across desks with no consolidated view of cost, let alone return.
A vendor business case reached the partner table and did not survive ten minutes of questions.
Capacity is the stated constraint while revenue per consultant sits flat, which means hours are going somewhere unbilled.
The next planning cycle needs an AI line item and there is no defensible number to put on it.

aiChanges: The cost side consolidates: one program cost, counted once, with each workflow carrying only its marginal cost.

Every number in the case traces to a source, because in a firm that sells judgment the business case is a work sample.

evidence.text: No approved primary source establishes search-firm operating economics or an AI outcome in executive search. The number this case needs does not exist in public.
evidence.caveat: Vendor predictions of hours saved circulate widely and are expectations respondents reported, not observed savings; they are excluded here rather than reframed. Only a baseline drawn from your own desks and honest measurement can show what governed AI returns.
